candidate.title: Is the Doctrine of Purgatory True? Trent Horn vs. James White (2024)
candidate.label: Purgatory and postmortem purification
candidate.summary: White wins by one point because his contextual exegesis and Romans argument slightly outweigh Horn's definitional clarification, purification syllogism, and historical continuity case.
candidate.motion: Is the doctrine of purgatory true?
candidate.sourceNote: Descriptions and quoted excerpts derive exclusively from the locked transcript inventory in packet.json; wording outside quotations is publication synthesis.
candidate.scoringNote: All overall, section, and move scores reproduce the frozen single deterministic score pass without recalculation, adjustment, or editorial override.

pro.name: The doctrine of purgatory is true
pro.speaker: Trent Horn

con.name: The doctrine of purgatory is false
con.speaker: James White

pro.text: Purgatory is the way Christ completes our sanctification
pro.context: Horn uses this formulation while defining purgatory as Christ's completion of holiness in already-saved persons, excluding both a second salvation opportunity and self-purification.

con.text: God imputes righteousness apart from works
con.context: White cites Romans 4 to ground righteous standing in credited righteousness through faith, making that text his controlling objection to purgatorial satisfaction and merit.

sections.title: Definition, satisfaction, and kinds of sin

pro.words: Horn defines purgatory as Christ's completion of sanctification for saved people, expressly excluding another chance at salvation and any process of sinners purifying themselves.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn identifies the proposition by distinguishing Christ-directed final sanctification from self-salvation or a renewed opportunity after condemnation, explaining the exceptional precision, relevance, and responsiveness marks. Principal limitation: His appeal to Protestant acceptance of sanctification establishes conceptual familiarity but offers comparatively little evidence that completion occurs through the specifically Catholic postmortem process, leaving evidence warrant below his presentation scores. Live burden: He must connect this bounded definition to biblical texts, theological consequences, and historical practices strongly enough to answer White's contention that satisfaction, punishment, merit, and indulgences belong essentially to the doctrine defended. Locked score: The 82 appropriately reflects precision clarity and relevance burden at 90, responsiveness at 86, coherent framing at 82, but thinner evidence warrant at 68 and moderate calibration charity at 78.

con.words: White counters that historic Catholic purgatory involves imposed suffering that atones for temporal punishment, so Horn's sanctification-only presentation understates the doctrine requiring defense.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White contests the affirmative at its definitional hinge by citing temporal punishment, purifying fire, and satisfaction, engaging Horn's narrowed account and justifying responsiveness and relevance scores. Principal limitation: The excerpt establishes that such language exists but does not demonstrate that passive satisfaction contradicts Christ-centered sanctification, while White's expression of surprise reduces charitable calibration toward Horn's explicit exclusions. Live burden: White must show that these components are essential to defeat the motion rather than compatible descriptions of gracious purification, and substantiate the theological incompatibility instead of relying on terminology. Locked score: The 83 matches responsiveness at 90 and relevance burden at 88, supported by logical coherence at 82 and precision clarity at 81, while evidence warrant at 77 and calibration charity at 74 constrain a stronger result.

pro.words: Horn answers White's atonement objection by distinguishing passive satis passio, in which God cleanses the soul, from personal work performed to earn departure from purgatory.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn answers White's definitional challenge by explaining satis passio as a passive divine operation, denying that souls perform compensatory labor to secure release. Principal limitation: This clarification resolves the self-cleansing allegation more effectively than the question whether imposed temporal suffering constitutes satisfaction additional to Christ's work, so the distinction does not settle historical components White introduced. Live burden: Horn must reconcile passive cleansing with treasury merit, indulgences, and punishment, demonstrating that these practices neither expand the defended doctrine nor compromise atonement's sufficiency. Locked score: The 83 reflects responsiveness at 89 and relevance burden at 87, with precision clarity at 84 and logical coherence at 81, while evidence warrant at 77 and calibration charity at 80 support but cannot elevate the answer beyond its definitional reach.

con.words: White argues that transferable excess merit and indulgent withdrawals cannot be reduced to ordinary divine rewards, preserving his broader historical definition against Horn's passive-process clarification.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White supplies institutional implications, connecting excess saintly merit to a treasury and indulgences, challenging Horn's passive-cleansing definition and his substitution of reward language for merit. Principal limitation: The rhetorical questions expose tension but do not independently establish the precise mechanics, authoritative status, or necessary relationship of those practices to defensible formulations of purgatory, limiting their evidentiary ceiling. Live burden: White must demonstrate that treasury and indulgence doctrines are inseparable from the motion's truth conditions and that Horn cannot distinguish their administration from the claim of postmortem purification. Locked score: The 83 is driven by responsiveness at 91 and relevance burden at 87, precision clarity at 83 and logical coherence at 82, while evidence warrant at 75 and calibration charity at 78 keep the reply appropriately bounded.

pro.words: Horn infers postmortem purification because some Christians die still desiring sin, whereas nobody entering heaven can retain any desire opposed to perfect holiness.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn presents the affirmative's cleanest inference: some saved Christians die retaining sinful desires, heaven excludes those desires, so purification must occur after death but before heavenly entrance. Principal limitation: This establishes a transition to perfected desire more securely than a temporally extended state of punishment, satisfaction, or other disputed Catholic particulars, explaining why evidence warrant trails logical structure. Live burden: Horn must show that this necessary transformation merits the doctrinal name purgatory and occupies the relevant postmortem interval, rather than occurring instantaneously through resurrection, judgment, or heavenly entrance itself. Locked score: The 84 rewards logical coherence at 84, responsiveness at 90, relevance burden at 91, and precision clarity at 88, with charitable calibration at 82, while evidence warrant at 74 records the underargued timing and mechanism.

con.words: White argues that believers stand before God clothed in Christ's seamless imputed righteousness, excluding purgatorial suffering or accumulated merit as grounds of acceptance.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White places Christ's imputed righteousness at the motion-level center, offering an alternative account of believers' standing before God and challenging reliance on purgatorial suffering or merit. Principal limitation: Righteous standing and completed sanctification are not identical, so this inference risks excluding a transformative process that Horn distinguishes from justification, weakening coherence and charitable calibration despite textual relevance. Live burden: White must prove that imputation eliminates every postmortem completion of holiness, not merely attempts to earn justification, and answer Horn's distinction between legal acceptance and the extinguishing of residual sinful desire. Locked score: The 78 reflects relevance burden at 85, responsiveness at 84, precision clarity at 80, and evidence warrant at 77, while logical coherence at 72 and calibration charity at 69 register the unresolved category distinction.

pro.words: Horn elicits White's agreement that sanctification may remain incomplete at death yet will be completed before heavenly entrance, securing common ground for postmortem transformation.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn secures the concession: White agrees sanctification may remain unfinished at death yet must be completed before heavenly entrance, supporting Horn's temporal case for postmortem purification. Principal limitation: Completion establishes neither unpleasant discipline, duration, satisfaction, nor Catholic doctrine, so this common ground does not show that White's transformation is purgatory rather than an immediate, distinct completion. Live burden: Horn must forge a doctrinally discriminating inference by demonstrating that White's completion and Catholic purification are relevantly identical, not merely verbally adjacent, while answering White's seamless-imputation account. Locked score: The 86 reflects evidence warrant at 88, responsiveness at 90, relevance burden at 88, precision clarity and calibration charity at 85 each, while logical coherence at 81 marks the remaining inferential distance from concession to the full motion.

con.words: White answers that believers already possess the new nature and may enter Christ's presence directly, so completed holiness does not require an intervening purgatorial state.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White answers Horn by pairing believers' new nature with direct entrance into Christ's presence, supplying a route from death to heaven without a purgatorial state. Principal limitation: Possessing a new nature does not explain how sinful desire disappears, while direct presence identifies the destination without proving transformation lacks logical or experiential priority, leaving coherence and warrant modest. Live burden: White must specify when and how unfinished sanctification becomes complete while preserving direct entrance, then show why completion cannot satisfy Horn's account of postmortem purification. Locked score: The 77 reflects responsiveness at 84 and relevance burden at 85, precision clarity at 78, evidence warrant and calibration charity at 73 each, while logical coherence at 71 records that White's paired assertions do not fully close Horn's transition argument.

pro.words: Horn closes by contrasting merely legal erasure with Christ's transforming love, which brings believers to complete sanctification and extinguishes every remaining trace of sin.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn returns to the motion through a Christological comparison: salvation culminates in transformation, directly answering White's imputation and direct-presence themes through completed sanctification. Principal limitation: Calling legal erasure a fiction underrepresents White's position, which includes regeneration and a new nature, while Horn's closing assertion supplies little fresh evidence for when or how transformation entails purgatory. Live burden: Horn still owes a demonstrated bridge from universally affirmed glorification to the disputed doctrine, including whether completion is disciplinary, temporally intermediate, or connected to satisfaction and consequences. Locked score: The 77 preserves strong relevance burden at 86, responsiveness at 84, precision clarity at 82, and logical coherence at 77, but evidence warrant at 71 and especially calibration charity at 61 penalize the unsupported contrast with White's account.

pro.words: Horn reasons that because some sinful Christians escape corrective discipline before dying, a perfecting God must sometimes administer unpleasant fatherly correction after death.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn offers an independent route beyond cleansing by inferring postmortem fatherly discipline when Christians die without receiving corrective consequences, directly engaging moral perfection and divine paternal governance. Principal limitation: The inference assumes every uncorrected earthly sin requires later unpleasant discipline and that perfection cannot occur through another gracious mode, while the cited pattern never establishes postmortem extension. Live burden: Horn must defend that universal corrective premise, distinguish therapeutic discipline from retributive satisfaction, and show why death cannot terminate the Hebrews-style process or complete its outstanding purposes through immediate glorification. Locked score: The 76 reflects responsiveness and relevance burden at 87, precision clarity at 85, and calibration charity at 72, but logical coherence at 68 and evidence warrant at 63 appropriately constrain an intuitive yet insufficiently demonstrated syllogism.

con.words: White argues that First John's sin unto death concerns apostasy, not Catholic mortal and venial categories, which he says the New Testament does not teach.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White directly contests Horn's biblical classification by construing First John's sin unto death as apostasy, challenging the scriptural warrant for later mortal and venial categories while squarely contacting Horn's defense. Principal limitation: Rejecting that Catholic taxonomy neither eliminates evident differences in sinful gravity nor independently defeats fatherly discipline, and White asserts New Testament absence without fully developing the competing exegesis. Live burden: White must demonstrate that Horn's practical distinction lacks alternative scriptural grounding and explain why unequal gravity or persistence cannot justify finite correction of already-saved believers. Locked score: The 78 reflects strong responsiveness at 85, precision clarity at 83, logical coherence at 80, and relevance burden at 78, while evidence warrant at 72 and calibration charity at 70 mark limited textual development and categorical dismissal.

pro.words: Horn distinguishes Christ's unique satisfaction of sin's eternal consequence from God's gentle fatherly restoration after Christians partially turn away, preserving finite corrective consequences.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn distinguishes eternal satisfaction, uniquely provided by Christ, from finite paternal restoration, directly answering White's concern that purgatorial consequences compete with the God-man's singular atonement. Principal limitation: The distinction is conceptually plausible but evidentially underdeveloped, because invoking an order of justice and gentle restoration does not establish that correction continues after death or corresponds to Catholic temporal punishment. Live burden: Horn must scripturally ground the eternal-versus-temporal division, derive postmortem correction from divine fatherhood rather than mere compatibility, and reconcile his gentle-restoration framing with harsher historical satisfaction language. Locked score: The 78 rewards responsiveness at 84, relevance burden at 85, precision clarity and calibration charity at 80, and logical coherence at 76, while evidence warrant at 66 limits a distinction whose scriptural and historical foundations remain undeveloped.

con.words: White confines Hebrews 12's fatherly discipline to earthly Christian life, denying Horn's extension of that passage to punishment or moral correction after death.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White confines Horn's principal Hebrews 12 analogy to the passage's textual setting, arguing that its fatherly discipline addresses living Christians and never states postmortem continuation, a source-specific limitation with substantial evidentiary force. Principal limitation: That immediate earthly application does not establish that divine fatherhood or correction ends at death, and it leaves Horn's independent claim about unpleasant postjudgment loss incompletely answered. Live burden: White must justify the exclusivity inference from present-life application to postmortem impossibility and explain how unfinished corrective purposes resolve without the unpleasant consequence Horn identifies. Locked score: The 82 reflects evidence warrant at 81, responsiveness at 86, relevance burden at 83, precision clarity at 85, logical coherence at 78, and calibration charity at 79, fitting a strong contextual limitation rather than comprehensive disproof.

pro.words: Horn appeals to the evident difference between recurring abortion and recurring minor sin to defend distinguishing grave from lesser wrongdoing within Christian moral life.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn uses a forceful comparison between repeated abortion and repeated minor wrongdoing to show that sins differ in gravity, lending the mortal versus venial distinction ordinary moral plausibility. Principal limitation: The illustration establishes neither Catholic categories nor their salvific consequences or connection to postmortem discipline, and it only obliquely addresses White's justification and sanctification distinction, matching the ledger's weakest responsiveness mark. Live burden: Horn must connect degrees of gravity to a scriptural taxonomy, then derive finite postmortem correction without assuming that familiar moral ranking validates every doctrinal consequence attached to those categories. Locked score: The 66 reflects logical coherence at 68, evidence warrant at 63, responsiveness at 58, relevance burden at 72, precision clarity at 74, and calibration charity at 65, matching this limited doctrinal defense.

pro.words: Horn secures White's acknowledgment that revealed loss of reward after death would feel bad, establishing at least one unpleasant consequence experienced by a saved person postmortem.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn secures White's precise concession that losing revealed rewards after death would feel bad, showing that a saved person can experience an unpleasant postmortem consequence despite White's ministry-context reading. Principal limitation: Regret over forfeited reward is not necessarily divine discipline, purification, satisfaction, temporal punishment, or a distinct purgatorial state, so this admission establishes less than the full doctrine. Live burden: Horn must demonstrate that the distress operates as morally perfecting correction within purgatory, rather than merely accompanying final evaluation without cleansing, satisfaction, or duration. Locked score: The 85 reflects logical coherence and evidence warrant at 84, responsiveness at 90, precision clarity at 87, and calibration charity at 85, while relevance burden at 80 captures the gap between a decisive local concession and the broader doctrinal conclusion.

pro.words: Horn reads Matthew 5's Gehenna context and release after the last penny as evidence of temporary punishment after death rather than ordinary civil imprisonment.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn connects Matthew 5's Gehenna warning with the prisoner's release after payment, using context and last-penny imagery to argue for finite postmortem punishment rather than merely worldly courts. Principal limitation: The legal exhortation may remain metaphorical or eschatological without specifying purgatory, while the payment image identifies neither who pays, what is purified, nor whether saved believers undergo the process. Live burden: Horn must establish that Gehenna is temporary here, exclude ordinary judicial warning and final condemnation, and connect release to the Catholic mechanism rather than generic postmortem accountability. Locked score: The 74 reflects responsiveness at 83, relevance burden at 80, and precision clarity at 79, while logical coherence at 69, evidence warrant at 67, and calibration charity at 70 capture unsupported correspondences across the interpretive chain.

con.words: White locates First Corinthians 3 within Paul's discussion of ministers building upon the Corinthian foundation, making tested ministry rather than purgatorial souls the passage's subject.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White grounds interpretation in Paul's sustained account of ministers building on his Corinthian foundation, identifying tested ministry as the concrete subject and directly challenging Horn's purgatorial reading. Principal limitation: That context does not exclude personal postmortem loss or an unpleasant judgment for the saved builder, so it narrows the passage's object without eliminating every consequence Horn infers. Live burden: White must explain salvation through fire, the builder's experienced loss, and why ministerial evaluation supplies neither direct nor analogical support for postmortem discipline. Locked score: The 86 integrates logical coherence at 85, evidence warrant at 84, responsiveness at 89, relevance burden at 88, precision clarity at 87, and calibration charity at 81, appropriately marking the section's strongest dimension pattern while preserving the unresolved consequence question.

pro.words: Horn argues that even a rewards-only interpretation leaves the saved builder suffering an unpleasant deprivation, because removal of a promised reward constitutes divine discipline.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn grants the rewards-only reading arguendo and shows that depriving someone of a promised reward remains an unpleasant divine consequence, preserving his disciplinary point without requiring explicit purification. Principal limitation: Calling forfeiture discipline does not establish cleansing, remission of temporal punishment, or occurrence in purgatory, and the inference assumes the reward was personally promised rather than conditionally available. Live burden: Horn must connect postjudgment loss to moral transformation and locate its timing relative to final judgment, entry into heaven, and the beatific vision. Locked score: The 81 reflects logical coherence at 80, responsiveness at 87, relevance burden at 82, precision clarity at 86, and calibration charity at 84, while evidence warrant at 72 appropriately restrains a resourceful fallback whose purgatorial significance remains indirect.

con.words: White presses Horn to identify how Matthew's judge, officer, prison, payment, and release imagery corresponds to purgatory rather than assuming legal language proves the doctrine.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White exposes Horn's missing inferential bridge by demanding how Matthew's judge, officer, prison, payment, and release correspond to a purgatorial mechanism, testing the complete legal imagery rather than isolated vocabulary. Principal limitation: His questions establish underdetermination but provide little positive contextual exegesis, weakening Horn's interpretation more clearly than they establish a superior non-purgatorial reading of Jesus' warning. Live burden: White must explain the Gehenna setting and last-penny release coherently, showing why temporary postmortem accountability does not best explain the sequence. Locked score: The 80 reflects logical coherence at 79, evidence warrant at 77, responsiveness at 82, relevance burden at 84, precision clarity at 76, and calibration charity at 79, appropriately rewarding a direct, calibrated burden challenge while recognizing its repetitive phrasing and incomplete interpretive precision.

pro.words: Horn answers the ministry-context objection by emphasizing the saved builder's loss and citing a Greek lexicon that classifies the relevant First Corinthians term as punishment.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn answers White's ministry-context reading with lexical evidence that the builder's loss can mean punishment, supporting judgment as more than disclosure of deficient ministerial work. Principal limitation: A punishment gloss establishes lexical possibility, not purification, while ministry context may still govern whose work is tested and why, leaving the loss's object, character, and doctrinal significance unclear. Live burden: Horn must show that punishment is contextually preferred and that a saved minister's punishment constitutes purgatorial correction rather than forfeiture of reward at final judgment. Locked score: The 78 reflects evidence warrant at 78, responsiveness at 84, relevance burden at 81, precision clarity at 77, logical coherence at 75, and calibration charity at 73, rewarding direct lexical contact while recognizing the incomplete inference from punitive loss to purgatory.

con.words: White maintains that First Corinthians 3 concerns revelation and testing rather than purification, while denying that Horn's disputed reading of loss establishes postmortem cleansing.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White keeps the distinction visible: First Corinthians 3 describes revelation and testing of work, not purification of a person, so Horn's doctrinal conclusion does not follow. Principal limitation: Calling the passage clear and rejecting the loss gloss does not fully answer Horn's fallback inference that unpleasant forfeiture constitutes discipline, leaving the reply responsive to the Corinthian moves but insufficiently precise and charitable about their strongest form. Live burden: White must explain salvation through fire and experienced loss, then demonstrate why neither phrase supports corrective postmortem consequence even absent personal cleansing. Locked score: The 76 preserves responsiveness and relevance burden at 85, logical coherence at 75, and evidence warrant at 70, while precision clarity at 71 and calibration charity at 67 penalize assertion where rebuttal was required.

pro.words: Horn answers the timing objection by placing negative consequences and purification at final judgment before the beatific vision, rather than requiring present souls to undergo them already.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn recognizes White's objection and offers a sequence in which final judgment, negative consequence, and purification precede the beatific vision, preserving space for the Corinthian day. Principal limitation: This answer does not reconcile final-day placement with claims about souls presently undergoing purgatory, and it asserts the sequence without textual demonstration or an account of intermediate-state timing, leaving its contact with White's challenge partial. Live burden: Horn must specify whether purgatory occurs after death, at general judgment, or in both settings, and demonstrate how First Corinthians supports that chronology rather than permitting it. Locked score: The 73 retains relevance burden at 78, precision clarity at 77, calibration charity at 74, responsiveness at 73, logical coherence at 72, and evidence warrant at 67, marking a but underdeveloped answer.

con.words: White observes that First Corinthians locates testing on the future day, whereas purgatory supposedly contains souls now, forcing Horn to supply an additional timing premise.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies the specific chronological mismatch between souls undergoing purgatory now and First Corinthians testing on the future day, forcing an unstated timing bridge. Principal limitation: The objection presumes Catholic chronology and does not exclude purification at individual judgment, final judgment, or a relation between them, so its force depends on definitions White has not established. Live burden: White must show that Horn necessarily places the Corinthian event before the scriptural day and cannot distinguish present intermediate purification from later public evaluation. Locked score: The 84 reflects logical coherence at 84, evidence warrant at 80, responsiveness at 91, relevance burden at 87, precision clarity at 82, and calibration charity at 76, recognizing a powerful direct challenge limited by assumptions about Horn's timeline.

pro.words: Horn argues that the repentant thief's fervor and torturous accepted death could remit every temporal consequence, making immediate paradise compatible with purgatory's general truth.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn answers the thief counterexample through complete remission by fervent repentance and accepted suffering, explaining why one saved person could enter paradise immediately without disproving a general purgatorial process. Principal limitation: This remission is possible within Horn's framework but not demonstrated from the thief narrative, which never states crucifixion or extraordinary contrition exhausted temporal consequences, leaving the inference underwarranted. Live burden: Horn must independently ground the remission principle and explain why the thief's physical punishment counts toward postmortem liabilities without making purgatory unfalsifiable through ad hoc exemptions. Locked score: The 79 reflects responsiveness at 88, relevance burden at 83, precision clarity at 81, calibration charity at 78, logical coherence at 75, and evidence warrant at 71, fitting a coherent exception whose decisive premises remain imported.

con.words: White answers that the thief simply trusted Christ and was saved perfectly, treating immediate paradise as evidence that faith needs no supplementary purgatorial remission.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White foregrounds the thief’s trust in Christ and Christ’s promise of paradise, presenting perfect salvation as a counterexample to any necessary purgatorial interval. Principal limitation: Horn does not claim every believer undergoes purgatory, while perfect salvation remains compatible with completed sanctification or remitted temporal consequences, so White’s reply only partially contacts Horn’s stated exception. Live burden: White must demonstrate that the thief retained relevant imperfections or temporal liabilities yet entered the beatific vision without purification, rather than establishing salvation, which Horn already grants. Locked score: The 73 preserves precision clarity at 80 and relevance burden at 79, alongside evidence warrant at 72 and calibration charity at 71, while logical coherence at 68 and responsiveness at 71 register the transition from perfect salvation to no postmortem transformation.

pro.words: Horn reads Christ's judgment seat, where everyone receives good or evil, as permitting postmortem punishment that could function toward purification before heavenly fulfillment.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn invokes Second Corinthians 5’s judgment-seat language, where persons receive good or evil according to deeds, providing a stronger chronological basis for adverse postmortem consequences than his inferential Matthew appeal. Principal limitation: The passage never identifies those consequences as temporary, therapeutic, or purifying, so deriving purgatorial punishment requires premises concerning the recipients’ salvation and judgment’s transformative function. Live burden: Horn must establish that recipients of adverse recompense remain destined for heaven and that this recompense purifies them, rather than merely declaring or penalizing their works. Locked score: The 77 rewards responsiveness at 85, relevance burden at 81, precision clarity at 79, and evidence warrant at 75, while calibration charity at 72 and logical coherence at 69 appropriately record the inferential gap between postmortem judgment and purification.

pro.words: Horn recasts Catholic merit as rewards freely granted by God, including benefits bestowed because of another believer's faithful goodness, rather than independent human earning.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn recasts merit as gracious divine reward, invoking New Testament interpersonal blessing to preserve God’s initiative over autonomous human earning and contact White’s Romans 4 objection. Principal limitation: The substitution neither explains excess transferable merit, treasury mechanics, or indulgences nor supplies textual evidence that Catholic technical usage is exhausted by reward language. Live burden: Horn must demonstrate that the historical doctrine actually uses merit derivatively and that benefits mediated through another’s faithfulness neither compromise Christ’s unique sufficiency nor introduce satisfaction by works. Locked score: The 75 reflects responsiveness at 79, relevance burden at 78, logical coherence and precision clarity at 75, calibration charity at 74, and evidence warrant at 69, fitting a plausible semantic repair that leaves White’s institutional counterexamples substantially unanswered.

con.words: White grounds the believer's blessed standing in Romans 4, where faith is credited as righteousness and God imputes righteousness apart from works.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White grounds his gospel-sufficiency argument in Romans 4’s explicit sequence of faith, credited righteousness, blessedness, and righteousness apart from works, establishing a textual principle against merit-based standing. Principal limitation: The passage establishes justification powerfully but does not itself determine whether justified believers require later sanctifying completion, so excluding every purgatorial model depends on the disputed relationship between standing and transformation. Live burden: White must show that Horn’s passive purification, finite consequences, and gracious rewards necessarily alter justification’s ground rather than describe consequences within an already-secured salvation. Locked score: The 85 reflects evidence warrant at 87, precision clarity at 89, relevance burden at 86, logical coherence at 85, responsiveness at 83, and calibration charity at 80, fitting exceptional textual control with one significant category bridge still unresolved.

pro.words: Horn argues that Christ's declaration of completion concerns his passion, not every salvific event, since resurrection remains necessary and is associated with believers' justification.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn carefully limits the inference from Christ's declaration that it is finished, distinguishing completion of the passion from completion of every salvific application and invoking resurrection for justification as concrete counterevidence. Principal limitation: Defeating an overbroad reading of the declaration does not positively establish purgatory, and the move does not show that postmortem punishment or satisfaction follows from salvation's multistage application. Live burden: Horn must connect the legitimate distinction among passion, resurrection, justification, sanctification, and glorification to a specifically purgatorial completion without implying deficiency in Christ's accomplished work. Locked score: The 81 reflects logical coherence and evidence warrant at 81, responsiveness and precision clarity at 84, relevance burden at 80, and calibration charity at 77, a strong corrective argument whose affirmative payoff remains limited.

con.words: White charges Catholic theology with confusing justification and sanctification, maintaining that imputed righteousness, not transformative cleansing, determines the believer's standing before God.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies the pivotal theological distinction between righteous standing and progressive transformation, explaining why imputed righteousness, rather than cleansing, governs acceptance before God and directly contests Horn's passive-purification clarification. Principal limitation: Labeling Horn's position a fundamental confusion does not demonstrate from Horn's stated premises that purification of already-saved people collapses sanctification into justification, while the excerpt offers no close doctrinal or textual evidence for that Catholic conflation. Live burden: White must establish the missing inference and explain why postmortem sanctification threatens complete justification even if it neither earns acceptance nor replaces Christ's imputed righteousness. Locked score: The 75 preserves strong relevance burden at 84 and coherence at 78, but responsiveness and clarity at 76 and evidence and charity at 67 reflect incomplete contact, support, and calibration.

pro.words: Horn insists Christ's death remains indispensable because only Christ satisfies sin's infinite eternal consequence and opens access to God, notwithstanding finite corrective consequences.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn preserves Christ's unique necessity by assigning satisfaction for sin's infinite eternal consequence exclusively to the God-man, while treating finite consequences as derivative of access Christ alone makes possible, thereby answering White's atonement objection. Principal limitation: This assertion neither establishes the eternal-temporal taxonomy nor explains how finite satisfaction avoids adding compensatory liability after complete atonement, leaving its doctrinal architecture clearer and more responsive than evidentially demonstrated. Live burden: Horn must ground the distinction textually and show how merit, indulgences, discipline, and purification remain derivative without becoming additional conditions of righteous standing or heavenly entrance. Locked score: The 82 reflects coherence at 83, responsiveness at 86, relevance at 85, clarity at 83, and charity at 84, while evidence warrant at 71 appropriately records stated but insufficiently supported premises.

con.words: White closes by making Romans 4's imputed righteousness apart from works the controlling gospel standard and directly rejecting Horn's characterization of imputation as legal fiction.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White closes on his strongest text, using Romans 4's imputation language to answer merit, Christ's necessity, and Horn's legal-fiction charge while keeping the motion's gospel comparison central. Principal limitation: The closing still treats transformation and imputed standing too nearly as mutually exclusive, and its sharp legal-fiction response insufficiently acknowledges Horn's claim that Christ both justifies and sanctifies. Live burden: White must prove every purgatorial consequence modifies justification rather than follows it, while explaining completed holiness without conceding Horn's minimal postmortem core. Locked score: The 84 reflects evidence warrant at 86, responsiveness at 87, relevance burden at 88, logical coherence and precision clarity at 82, while calibration charity at 70 properly limits a forceful synthesis that sometimes compresses the affirmative distinction.

pro.words: Horn cites Jewish Gehenna tradition as pre-Christian precedent for souls undergoing purgation before entering God's supernatural realm, supplying conceptual continuity rather than direct Christian proof.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn introduces pre-Christian Jewish precedent describing Gehenna as purgation followed by entrance into God's realm, showing that temporary postmortem purification was conceptually available within a relevant religious environment. Principal limitation: The cited scholarly summary does not establish the tradition's date, authority, uniformity, or influence upon apostolic Christianity, and Jewish precedent alone cannot prove a specifically Catholic doctrine. Live burden: Horn must connect this tradition historically or textually to Jesus and the early church, distinguishing genuine antecedent evidence from a later parallel that merely resembles purgatory. Locked score: The 76 reflects precision clarity at 82, responsiveness at 81, logical coherence at 76, evidence warrant and relevance burden at 73, and calibration charity at 68, fitting a useful contextual precedent whose genealogy and doctrinal significance remain uncertain.

con.words: White argues that the developed doctrine emerged across roughly fourteen centuries and was absent from Horn's earliest witnesses, despite those writers containing scattered afterlife concepts.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White frames a precise historical burden by distinguishing scattered early motifs from the developed doctrine and noting a roughly fourteen-century process, directly challenging claims of continuous apostolic teaching. Principal limitation: Development over time does not itself imply falsity, and the move relies upon a broad historical assertion without displaying enough primary evidence or defining which doctrinal features must appear earliest. Live burden: White must show discontinuity rather than maturation, identify the indispensable late additions, and explain why early purification or temporary-punishment testimony cannot constitute a genuine doctrinal core. Locked score: The 79 reflects responsiveness at 86, precision clarity at 80, logical coherence and relevance burden at 79, calibration charity at 77, and evidence warrant at 73, appropriately rewarding the central historical distinction while limiting its evidentiary completeness.

pro.words: Horn cites Clement's sanctifying nonconsuming fire and Augustine's temporary punishments after death as early Christian witnesses to a postmortem purifying or corrective core.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn supplies named early Christian witnesses and specific concepts, Clement's sanctifying nonconsuming fire and Augustine's temporary postmortem punishments, moving beyond abstract possibility toward historical continuity. Principal limitation: These statements do not establish agreement on subjects, mechanism, duration, satisfaction, or later dogmatic particulars, while reliance on summarized citations limits verification and permits substantial diversity beneath similar vocabulary. Live burden: Horn must show that the witnesses express one recognizable doctrinal core rather than distinct speculative eschatologies and explain which later Catholic elements legitimately develop from them. Locked score: The 79 reflects precision clarity and responsiveness at 82, relevance burden at 79, logical coherence at 78, evidence warrant at 77, and calibration charity at 72, a strong but qualified historical showing whose continuity claim exceeds the displayed evidence.

con.words: White replies that diverse patristic afterlife theories were only distilled into the later Catholic doctrine during the fifteenth century, undermining claims of early doctrinal identity.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White directly answers Horn's named witnesses by distinguishing diverse early perspectives from the fifteenth-century dogmatic distillation, giving historical variation a clear argumentative consequence for claims of continuity. Principal limitation: Diversity is compatible with development around a shared core, and the move offers little specific comparison among Clement, Augustine, Florence, and later catechetical formulations to establish substantive discontinuity. Live burden: White must identify contradictions or absent essentials rather than mere terminological variety, then explain why later synthesis cannot legitimately preserve the early purifying and temporary-punishment strands Horn documented. Locked score: The 80 reflects responsiveness at 88, logical coherence and precision clarity at 81, relevance burden and calibration charity at 80, but evidence warrant at 71 appropriately limits a well-targeted historical thesis whose comparative documentation remains thin.

pro.words: Horn argues that sanctification and satisfaction models converge when purification itself constitutes temporary punishment, allowing diverse formulations to develop around one postmortem core.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Horn offers a charitable synthesis of historical diversity, proposing that sanctification and satisfaction converge when the purification itself constitutes finite punishment, thereby directly answering White's development objection. Principal limitation: The convergence is conceptually possible but historically underdemonstrated, and identifying two descriptions as complementary does not show that particular fathers, councils, or magisterial sources understood them as one process. Live burden: Horn must provide documentary links establishing continuity and explain how treasury merit and indulgences fit the synthesis without expanding it beyond passive purification. Locked score: The 78 reflects responsiveness at 85, calibration charity at 85, relevance burden at 81, logical coherence at 77, precision clarity at 74, and evidence warrant at 70, accurately rewarding an integrative reply whose historical proof and formulation remain incomplete.

con.words: White concedes Augustine's language about postmortem purgatorial punishment while carefully distinguishing that early statement from the doctrine later defined by the Council of Florence.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White makes a precise and unusually charitable concession that Augustine used postmortem purgatorial language, then narrows the issue to whether Augustine possessed the doctrine later defined at Florence. Principal limitation: The distinction establishes incomplete development more readily than contradiction, and conceding the core language strengthens Horn unless White specifies which later essentials alter rather than clarify Augustine's position. Live burden: White must compare Augustine and Florence point by point, demonstrating that the conceded antecedent cannot support legitimate continuity or the motion's minimal purifying claim. Locked score: The 85 reflects logical coherence at 85, responsiveness at 91, relevance burden and precision clarity at 83, evidence warrant at 78, and exceptional calibration charity at 90, a disciplined concession whose high quality does not itself complete the larger discontinuity argument.

con.words: White closes that Catholic scholarship reveals scattered early elements shaped through Clement and Origen rather than a continuous pure biblical stream supporting the mature doctrine.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White synthesizes the historical negative by treating early evidence as scattered elements and invoking scholarly development through Clement and Origen rather than simple apostolic transmission. Principal limitation: Referring listeners to scholarship without presenting decisive comparisons weakens the evidence, while calling the stream impure risks prejudging philosophical influence instead of demonstrating doctrinal error or discontinuity. Live burden: White must substantiate how Clement and Origen transformed biblical materials, identify resulting nonbiblical commitments, and answer Horn's claim that divergent models converge around a legitimate purifying core. Locked score: The 79 reflects responsiveness at 87, relevance burden at 80, logical coherence and precision clarity at 79, evidence warrant at 74, and calibration charity at 72, fitting an effective synthesis whose documentation remains underdeveloped and characterization sharpened.

strengths: Horn's narrow, precise definition framed purgatory as Christ's passive completion of sanctification, clearly excluding any second chance, self-purification, or salvation achieved independently of Christ.
His postmortem cleansing syllogism clearly connected unfinished sinful desire at death with heaven's perfect holiness, establishing the affirmative's strongest conceptual necessity argument.
Horn elicited White's important concession that sanctification unfinished at death is completed before heavenly entrance, securing unusually strong direct evidence for postmortem transformation.
His Augustine, Clement, and Jewish evidence established a recognizable historical precedent for purifying fire or temporary punishment, even though later doctrinal continuity remained disputed.

blunders.text: Horn's recurring appeal to mortal and venial gravity used an intuitive abortion comparison but did not answer White's justification objection or establish the Catholic taxonomy scripturally.
His Matthew last-penny reading left judge, prison, payment, saved status, and purification correspondences underargued, making a suggestive legal image carry excessive doctrinal weight.
Calling imputed righteousness a legal fiction underrepresented White's regeneration and new-nature claims, sharply lowering charity and distracting from Horn's stronger completion argument.

strengths: White's ministry-context reading of First Corinthians 3 supplied the debate's strongest integrated exegesis, explaining Paul's foundation, builders, works, fire, and evaluative setting.
His Romans 4 argument grounded righteous standing in imputation apart from works, giving the negative a stable textual principle across merit, satisfaction, and closing exchanges.
White's final-day timing challenge exposed an additional premise required to connect present purgatorial souls with First Corinthians' future day of testing and disclosure.

White's qualified concession on Augustine showed exceptional responsiveness and charity: he acknowledged Augustine's postmortem purgatorial language while precisely distinguishing it from Florence's fully developed doctrine.

blunders.text: White repeatedly moved from complete justification to the absence of postmortem sanctification without fully proving that righteous standing and transformative completion are mutually exclusive.
His thief reply affirmed perfect salvation but incompletely contacted Horn's claim that exceptional repentance and suffering could remit temporal consequences before immediate paradise.
The closing historical claim invoked scholarly development and an impure stream without presenting enough comparative evidence to demonstrate discontinuity rather than legitimate maturation.

finalArgument.thesis: Purgatory is best understood as Christ's gracious postmortem completion of holiness and fatherly correction in saved persons who die reconciled but morally unfinished.
premises: No person enjoying the beatific vision can retain a disordered desire, unresolved resistance to goodness, or moral condition incompatible with complete communion with God.
Many reconciled Christians die while still possessing disordered desires and unfinished sanctification, so some divinely caused transformation must occur after their earthly lives end.
A transformation occurring after death and before complete heavenly communion satisfies purgatory's minimal purifying core even if its duration is instantaneous or phenomenology remains unspecified.

Scripture's judgment, loss, recompense, and fatherly-discipline patterns make an unpleasant corrective aspect coherent without converting finite consequences into a second atonement or self-salvation.

Early Jewish and Christian purification traditions are diverse, yet their recurring postmortem purgation and temporary-punishment themes provide cumulative continuity rather than isolated conceptual coincidence.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore the affirmative core is more probable: Christ may complete sanctification and finite correction after death without compromising justification, atonement, or the certainty of salvation.

newArguments.title: Personal identity requires healed agency
newArguments.text: Glorification must preserve the believer as the same responsible person rather than replace that person with an unrelated perfected subject. If deeply habituated desires structure agency at death, their removal plausibly involves a personally appropriated encounter with divine truth, not merely an external declaration. Such appropriation can be wholly caused by grace while still exposing and healing disordered attachments. A postmortem encounter of this kind supplies a philosophical basis for purification that neither earns salvation nor competes with Christ. It explains why perfected identity can involve correction rather than instantaneous discontinuity.

newArguments.title: Reconciliation and rehabilitation differ
newArguments.text: Legal reconciliation can be complete while rehabilitation remains unfinished, as pardon restores relationship without instantly repairing every disposition produced by wrongdoing. Christian salvation already distinguishes initiation, progressive sanctification, and final glorification without dividing Christ's work. Extending that rehabilitative completion beyond biological death is therefore not an additional sacrifice but the final application of one accomplished redemption. This model also explains why unpleasant recognition of harm may be medicinal: truthfully confronting one's effects can participate in healing while forgiveness remains secure. Purgatory becomes completed rehabilitation within reconciliation, not payment for admission.

newArguments.title: Communal repair before perfect communion
newArguments.text: Sin damages not only the sinner's interior state but also relationships within the redeemed community. Perfect communion plausibly requires each person to understand, renounce, and receive healing for those relational distortions, including harms never recognized during earthly life. Divine judgment can reveal these truths without threatening salvation, while grace transforms shame into restored love. This communal dimension explains why purification may involve painful disclosure yet culminate in joy rather than retribution. It reinforces purgatory as ecclesial repair: Christ prepares reconciled persons to participate transparently in a communion where concealed injury and defensive self-deception cannot remain.

finalArgument.thesis: The doctrine of purgatory should be rejected unless revelation establishes more than final glorification, because justification, direct presence, and contextual exegesis already explain the cited evidence.
premises: Romans presents the believer's righteous standing as God's imputation through faith apart from works, leaving no outstanding compensatory liability that merits or indulgences must discharge.
Texts promising presence with Christ and exemplifying the thief's immediate paradise naturally indicate direct entrance, while final transformation can occur without an intervening punitive state.
First Corinthians 3 tests ministerial work on the future day; its fire reveals quality and produces reward loss, but the passage never says a saved person is purified.
Hebrews 12 addresses embodied earthly discipline, and Matthew's legal imagery lacks the correspondences needed to identify a postmortem prison, purifying payment, or saved population.

Diverse early speculations and later dogmatic synthesis demonstrate historical development, while scattered similarities cannot substitute for apostolic teaching of the mature doctrine's essential structure.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore final glorification may be affirmed without purgatory, while punitive satisfaction, transferable merit, and the proposed scriptural mechanisms remain insufficiently established and unnecessary.

newArguments.title: Doctrinal economy favors glorification
newArguments.text: If two accounts explain the same transition to perfect holiness, the account introducing fewer unsupported states and mechanisms has an evidential advantage. Immediate glorification already explains how a believer dies imperfect yet enters heavenly communion perfected. Purgatory adds an intervening condition, possible suffering, temporal liabilities, and historically associated remissions without a text clearly requiring those additions. Conceptual compatibility is not enough when the motion asserts truth. Unless the added structure predicts or explains evidence that immediate glorification cannot, doctrinal economy favors affirming completed sanctification while withholding the purgatorial label and its disputed implications.

newArguments.title: Public judgment need not imply private purification
newArguments.text: Final judgment can disclose the moral truth of each life, vindicate divine justice, and assign differentiated rewards without changing the justified person's moral status through punishment. Public revelation serves communal and cosmic purposes distinct from private rehabilitation. Consequently, regret or loss at judgment does not entail an antecedent purgatorial process; it may be an aspect of truthful evaluation within already-perfected communion. This distinction absorbs Horn's strongest concession about feeling bad while denying the further inference to discipline that cleanses. Negative experience, moral evaluation, and purification are separate predicates, and the first two do not logically establish the third.

newArguments.title: Institutional consequences test the minimal definition
newArguments.text: A definition restricted to Christ completing sanctification risks becoming too minimal to vindicate the historical doctrine whose truth is debated. The treasury of merit, indulgences, temporal satisfaction, and specified punishments shaped purgatory's ecclesial operation and devotional significance. If these features are detachable errors, proving only a generic postmortem transformation does not rescue the larger doctrine; if they are essential, they require independent biblical and theological defense. This dilemma prevents equivocation between a broadly shared glorification claim and the contested Catholic system. The negative can grant transformation while denying that the concession establishes purgatory as historically taught.
